the Abiquiu is a fluvial deposit of Oligo-Miocenic age that was deposited in an intermontane basin that formed during the uplift of the Jemez Mountains.
the Abiquiu formation consists of three members: the basal conglomerate member, the limestone member, and the tuff member, in ascending stratigraphic order.
the Abiquiu is composed of three lithologically distinct units: (1) a basal conglomerate, (2) a middle unit of flinty limestone, and (3) an upper unit of flint chert.

the stratigraphy and sedimentology of the Abiquuiu Formation and the origin of the Pedernal Chert in the Espanola Basin.
the stratigraphy and petrology of the Abiquui Formation in north-central New Mexico and its relationship to basin evolution in the area.
the petrology, stratigraphy, and sedimentology of the Abiquui Formation.

the stratigraphic and petrologic relationships of the Santa Fe Group, and specifically the Abiquiu, are poorly understood.
the “Abiquii Formation” consists of the basal conglomerate (Pedernal Chert), the limestone, and a tuffaceous sandstone.
the Abiquiu is a poorly understood, but widely distributed unit of the Santa Fe Group, which is composed of three members.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the Abiquiu is a thick, complex, heterogeneous, sedimentary sequence, with the lower 200 m (650 ft) consisting of a basal conglomerate, overlain by a thick sequence of tuffaceous sandstone, tuffaceous mudstone, and tuffaceous shale, and capped by the distinctive Pedernal Chert (Figs. 2-5).
the Abiquiu is an important unit in the stratigraphic and tectonic evolution of north-central NewMexico.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there are two units in the Abiquiu, not three, and that the Abiquiu is a very thick unit.
the Abiquiu is not limited to the Esgana Basin, as previously thought, but extends westward into the San Pedro Basin.
